segments.title: Passion as a guide and a source of bias
segments.summary: A personal connection can make historical research compelling, but it can also steer a researcher toward a preferred reading of the evidence.
segments.body: Passion can be a strong reason to study history, but it can also harden into bias and make a researcher see more in the sources than they contain. The route into naval history began with tracing a family's military service. Roughly 100 relatives went to World War I and about 120 went to World War II, serving with British, Australian, New Zealand, Canadian, South African, American, and, in one case, French forces. Many chose dangerous roles involving fighter aircraft, commando operations, destroyers, or submarines, and many died. Following those lives turned a family inquiry into a much wider study of military and naval history across several countries. The personal connection supplies the questions and the motivation, while the surviving evidence still sets the limits of the conclusions.

evidence.note: He describes passion for history, warns that it can create bias, and explains how family service in both world wars led him into naval history.

segments.title: Uncle Sid and the limits of wartime blame
segments.summary: A family loss at sea becomes a caution against blaming one commander without tracing the incomplete information and decisions across the chain of command.
segments.body: Sid was a Fleet Air Arm fighter pilot travelling through the Indian Ocean to join his squadron when his ship was sunk by a German surface raider. The admiral responsible for the area had sent ships to hunt the raider in the wrong place, using the best information available because higher command had not passed along everything he needed. After the ship's gun crew was killed, Sid and his best friend took over the weapon and kept firing while others escaped in the lifeboats. His friend's fate is unknown. Sid washed ashore in India and was buried somewhere along the coast. The grave has yet to be located, though a visit is planned once it is found. Sid's sister later lost all three of her brothers, so her daughters grew up without uncles. The account does not assign sole blame to the admiral and instead traces the outcome through incomplete intelligence and decisions made across the chain of command, while keeping the human cost in view.

evidence.note: He describes Sid, the Indian Ocean sinking, the search for a German raider, and the commander acting without all the information he needed.
He rejects treating the admiral as solely responsible and reflects on the human cost to his family.
